note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, wording: The list of the five food groups uses commas both between groups and within group names, so it reads as many more than five groups. Students cannot tell where one group ends and the next begins. Semicolons or a numbered list would fix this.
- Question b, other: The clue 'with plenty of vegetables' points straight to the only option that contains vegetables, so it gives the answer away.
- Question b, level: Too easy for Year 11. The three wrong options are obvious junk-food meals, so the question does not test knowledge of the plate's proportions or food groups.

rejected.title: The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating
card: The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating is a plate graphic. It shows the proportions of the five food groups to eat each day. A bigger area on the plate means more food from that group.
The five food groups are vegetables and legumes, fruit, grain foods, lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts, seeds and legumes, and milk, yoghurt, cheese and alternatives.
Vegetables and legumes and grain foods take the largest areas of the plate. Fruit, the dairy group and the lean meats group take smaller areas.

Small amounts of unsaturated oils and spreads are shown beside the plate. Discretionary foods, such as cakes, soft drinks, hot chips and fried takeaway, are not in the five groups, so they sit off the plate.
rejected.remember: Vegetables and grain foods take the most space. Discretionary foods sit off the plate.

a.q: What does the size of each section on the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating show?
opts: The proportion of that food group to eat each day
The number of kilojoules in that food group
The price of foods in that food group
The order in which to eat the food groups
a.why: The plate shows proportions, so a larger section means more of that group in a day's eating. It does not measure kilojoules, which is a tempting guess because energy is part of nutrition.
a.clue: Think about what a bigger slice of the plate tells you.

b.q: Priya wants her dinner to match the guide. Which meal fits best?
opts: Grilled fish, brown rice and a large serve of vegetables
Fried chicken pieces with a large serve of hot chips
A large bowl of ice cream topped with chocolate sauce
Two slices of cake with a large glass of soft drink
b.why: Fish is in the lean meats group, brown rice is a grain food, and a large serve of vegetables matches the plate. Fried chicken and hot chips are discretionary foods, not serves from the five groups, and so are the ice cream, cake and soft drink.
b.clue: Look for a meal built from the five groups, with plenty of vegetables.

problems.detail: Saying lean meats and alternatives take a smaller area than fruit and the dairy group may not match the official plate graphic. On the graphic, the lean meats segment looks about the same size as dairy, and fruit looks smallest or similar. Check this against the AGHE image, or reword to 'vegetables and grain foods take the largest areas; fruit, dairy and lean meats take smaller areas'.

The why says the fried chicken and chips meal has 'too little from the vegetable group'. Chips come from potato, a vegetable, but are treated as a discretionary food. The why would be clearer saying fried foods and chips are discretionary rather than a vegetable serve. Calling fish a 'lean meat alternative' is also slightly off, because fish is in the lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs group itself.

opts: How much food to eat from that group each day
How many kilojoules are in that group's foods
How much foods in that group usually cost

a.why: The plate shows proportions, so a larger section means more of that group in a day's eating. It does not measure kilojoules, which is a tempting guess because energy is part of nutrition.

b.q: Jaya's dinner plate is half cooked vegetables, with a small serve of baked salmon and a small serve of rice. Compared with the guide, what is the best change?
opts: Add a serve of grain foods such as more rice or pasta
Swap the salmon for a larger serve of fish and eggs
Replace the vegetables with a glass of fruit juice
Add a small serve of chips from the discretionary group
b.why: The guide gives grain foods a large area, so a small serve of rice is too little. More fish would shrink a group that has a smaller area, and chips are discretionary foods that sit off the plate.
b.clue: Compare each group's size on her plate with its area on the guide.

a.best: How much food to eat from that group each day

b.best: Add a serve of grain foods such as more rice or pasta

problems.detail: Why (b) says more fish 'would shrink a group that has a smaller area'. More fish would enlarge the lean meats group beyond its small area, not shrink it. This could confuse students about the reasoning.

The distractor 'Swap the salmon for a larger serve of fish and eggs' is confusing, because salmon is already a fish. It reads as a swap within the same group rather than a clear wrong choice. Wording such as 'Make the salmon serve much larger' would be clearer.

The guide shows proportions across a whole day's eating, but the question judges a single dinner plate against it without saying so. This could teach that every meal must match the plate. The question could say it treats the dinner as a guide to balance.
